knowledge_type_note: A meta-record about the strategic ideas that carry a person's name, and what this base has found when it checked the names.

history.notes: A meta-record summarising this base's own attribution findings; each individual claim is documented on its own concept.

engine_era_note: Engines settle whether a named rule is TRUE, which is a different question from who said it. Tarrasch's rule is the case where both were checked and both came back negative: the attribution is disputed and the rule is false as stated.

preconditions: An idea is about to be attributed to a person
recognition.detector: the history.attributions block, enforced by tools/schema.json
false_positive_traps: A name attached to a concept is a claim about history and needs a source like any other claim. This base's checked attributions came back wrong or disputed more often than they came back clean.
Popularising is not originating, and the schema separates them precisely because conflating them is how misattributions start.
An attribution being widespread is not evidence. The Lucena misattribution has been repeated since 1880.

typical_plans: Record the relation, not just the name
Keep competing claims side by side rather than choosing
Say unknown where the trail runs out

exceptions: Some attributions are solid: the gambit etymology traces to Ruy Lopez in 1561 with Lopez's own derivation quoted, and Nimzowitsch's prophylaxis and overprotection are his beyond dispute.
limitations: This base's historical research is English-language and second-hand in most cases; several primary texts were consulted through summaries and each such source note says so.
Absence of a recorded dispute means this base has not found one, not that none exists.

NO REGISTERED FALSE-POSITIVE CASE, because this record is about the BASE rather than about boards. It is an index over other concepts, and the conditions it states are conditions on how this system names and files things - not patterns a position can exhibit. A false-positive case here would have to be a mis-filed concept rather than a mistaken reading of a board, and that is what tools/audit.py and tools/validate_kb.py check, on every record, on every run. Recorded rather than filled: tools/depth_report.py still counts this concept as missing the item, and the completion assessment carries the gap.
misconceptions: That a name on a chess idea records who thought of it. It usually records who popularised it in a particular language.
That widely repeated attributions have been checked. The Lucena misattribution dates from 1880 and is still repeated.

by_level.beginner: Lots of chess ideas are named after people who did not invent them.
by_level.intermediate: Named strategic ideas usually record who popularised them, not who found them.
by_level.advanced: When this base checked its attributions, most came back disputed or wrong — the Lucena position is not Lucena's, and Tarrasch's rule may be Tartakower's and is false as stated anyway.
by_level.master: Every attribution here carries a relation and a confidence, and competing claims sit side by side rather than being resolved by preference.

by_depth.short: Strategic ideas named after people — usually the wrong people.
by_depth.normal: Ideas that carry a person's name, and the finding that checking the name usually changes the story: the Lucena position is not in Lucena's book, the worst-piece rule has four different names, and Tarrasch's rook rule is both disputed and false as stated.
by_depth.deep: Chess attaches names to ideas readily and checks them rarely, and when this base checked, the attributions usually did not survive intact. The Lucena position is not in Lucena's 1497 book and the error is traceable to an 1880 handbook. The principle of two weaknesses is Nimzowitsch's idea under another word while the name travels through three other people. The worst-piece rule has four names, one of them after a player who never stated it. Why it happens is ordinary - names attach to whoever popularised an idea in a language, and citations get copied rather than checked - and it matters because repeating attributions confidently teaches things that are not true.

explanations.lesson: A name on an idea is a historical claim. Check it, or record it as unverified.

avoid: the X position, discovered by X

definition_short: Strategic ideas attached to a person's name — and the finding that the attribution is wrong or disputed more often than not.
definition_long:
Chess attaches names to strategic ideas readily and checks them rarely. This base checked, and the results are consistent enough to be worth stating as a general finding: WHEN AN ATTRIBUTION IS CHECKED IT USUALLY DOES NOT SURVIVE INTACT.

WHAT THE CHECKING FOUND, each recorded in full on its own concept:
- THE LUCENA POSITION is not in Lucena's 1497 book. Salvio credits Genovino in 1634, and the misattribution is traceable to Schwede's 1880 Handbuch.
- TARRASCH'S RULE about the rook behind the passed pawn is disputed between Tarrasch and Tartakower, and is DISPROVED as a general rule by this base's own Vancura pair.
- THE PRINCIPLE OF TWO WEAKNESSES is Nimzowitsch's idea under a different word — he has it as 'tacking' — while the NAME travels Belavenets to Dvoretsky to Shereshevsky.
- THE WORST-PIECE RULE has four names: Anderssen's, Makogonov's, Fischer's (from Botvinnik, though Fischer never stated it) and Dvoretsky's 'principle of the worst piece'.
- 'THE BEST WAY TO REFUTE A GAMBIT IS TO ACCEPT IT' drifts between 'gambit' and 'sacrifice' across sources and is doubtfully Steinitz's, who separately said declining is not cowardice.
- STEINITZ'S OWN THEORY may be Paulsen's in its key proposition, on one source's account.
- ZUGZWANG's coinage is 'alleged' to Max Lange, per Winter.

WHY IT HAPPENS is ordinary: names attach to whoever POPULARISED an idea in a given language, citations get copied rather than checked, and a memorable attribution outlives the correction. None of it is scandalous and all of it matters, because a base that repeats attributions confidently is teaching things that are not true.

THE PRACTICE THAT FOLLOWS: every attribution here carries a RELATION rather than a bare name — originated-by, first-documented-by, popularized-by, named-by, later-associated-with — plus a confidence, and competing claims are recorded side by side rather than resolved by preference. Where the trail runs out the record says unknown.

The corresponding check exists and runs on every record on every commit - tools/validate_kb.py for structure and naming, tools/audit.py for source discipline and stage promotion - which is the right instrument for a claim about the base.
